This is a strong record, but I think the Lifou Palm has an even better story than the JSON currently lets it tell. The combination of tiny range, unusual limestone habitat, white woolly crownshaft, and conservation work is excellent.
A few things I'd change.

The biggest opportunity: make the limestone story more vivid
Your second quick hit is potentially the best fact in the record:
“It is the only palm in the world that grows naturally on the raised coral limestone of the Loyalty Islands…”
But “only palm in the world” is broader than necessary and potentially risky. Your origin version is more precise:
“the only New Caledonian palm that grows on raised coral limestone substrate”
I'd use that.
And I'd explain why the geology matters:

events.summary: The record has been substantially restructured around the five priorities the reviewer identified: tiny wild population (corrected to 'fewer than 100' from the unsupported 113-tree figure), the white woolly crownshaft, limestone geological specialization (with 'nutrient-poor' removed after the IRD paper showed Lifou limestone soils are actually organically rich), the Jozip community conservation effort, and the genus's uniqueness on the Loyalty Islands. The 1976 description fact has moved from quick_hits into more_information, speculative wildlife language has been replaced with honest uncertainty, and several editorial judgments have been removed or reframed.

events.feedback:
Yes. This is very close. I’d make a few final content-level changes before calling the Lifou Palm entry done.
1. The strongest quick hit should be even stronger
Your first hit is good, but I’d make the conservation punch more immediate and less hedged:
The entire known wild range of this palm occupies only about 8 square kilometers on one small island, with fewer than 100 mature individuals estimated in the wild. The palm in front of you may be more numerous in cultivation than in its native forest.
That last sentence is memorable and communicates the astonishing conservation story without sounding melodramatic.
I would keep this as Quick Hit #1.
2. I would soften the “no surface water” claim
This:
“the island has no surface water at all”
is vivid, but it's also the sort of absolute geographical statement I'd be reluctant to put into a permanent botanical record unless you have a particularly strong source for it.
